cadence

3 claims
Candidate Law cadence · Maker / build
moderate Reproduced The same relationship showed up on independent channels. Much harder to explain as coincidence — still not a demonstrated cause. held 63% of 24 measurements 8 channels
Find a stable upload cadence and keep it, so the channel becomes part of viewers' weekly patterns; consistency of rhythm matters, not just raw frequency.
Source: Mario Joos
Reviewed by the team’s strategist

Merged 1 duplicate (2026-09-01): The duplicate additionally asserted consistency matters MORE THAN the interval itself — a comparative no current probe tests. If a probe ever compares the two, that claim deserves re-opening as its own question. Decomposed into 2 atomic claims by our strategist (directed in chat 2026-09-02, executed by Claude) (2026-09-02).

Evidence and caveats →
Measurement record

Tested as: shipping on the channel's usual rhythm → first-28-day views vs off-rhythm uploads (the claim predicts this goes up)

The question put to the data: On this channel, do uploads that arrived on the channel's usual rhythm out-perform ones that broke it?

Exact arithmetic: Median first-28-day views for uploads arriving within half the channel's typical 48.0-day gap, minus the same for uploads that broke the rhythm.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up. One dot per channel — 146 earlier readings were superseded by a later re-measurement of the same channel and are not drawn.

Measured refinement — Median days between uploads per channel (40 most recent uploads)

Measured directly: the median channel uploads every 14 days (middle half 7-27.8). The claim is about KEEPING a rhythm, not about its length; this shows what rhythms the fleet actually runs, which is the range any "weekly" advice has to survive.

Window: 228 channels with 8+ dated uploads; gaps over the 40 most recent. Each dot is one channel's median; hover a dot for its name.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Contradicted: Brief: superlative delta -0.06 (maker-builds, n=21), -0.01 (motorcycle, n=48), -0.05 (roblox, n=51) — negative in all three niches. My corpus check across 46 channels: WITH n=21 median 1.01x vs 1.00x (p=0.71); age-adjusted 0.98x vs 1.00x (p=0.52); 1 of 3 channels with >=2 matches came out ahead. Our own channels: n=4, median 0.75x. The library agrees: 'The World's Most ___' 1.09x, "World's Most ___ People" 0.98x, 'I Made the World's Most <SUPERLATIVE> <THING>' 0.84x — three of the four lowest-lift formats we have mined. Channel G' 'I built "the world's best speakers"' returned 0.75x against his own median.

Caveat: Title keywords are an imperfect stand-in for a genuinely superlative SUBJECT — a video can be about the world's largest thing without saying so in the title. Sample sizes for the tight regex are small (n=21 corpus, n=4 ours) even though three independent measurements agree on direction. The claim's premise (no direct competition) is not itself tested; only its performance consequence is.

Where the claim came from

A near-duplicate of a proven format outperforms a wholly new one because familiarity does the work of removing risk while a small novel element supplies the reason to click — roughly a 90/10 split of template to twist.
Source: Alan Garnett
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

WHERE ON THE EXPOSURE CURVE is this format for this audience? Gannett already holds the reconciling pattern (115f4acc5069): liking follows an inverted-U against exposure count, rising with repetition to a peak and falling after, so a format has a finite number of uses. Both claims are true, on opposite sides of the peak — which converts an argument into a measurement problem: what is the instalment count, and is per-instalment performance still rising? Our mined-format table is weakly consistent with the decay side and worth watching rather than citing: the highest observed lifts sit on small match counts (I Built My Own After Getting Screwed, n=4, 2.92x; Exposing N Secrets, n=3, 2.76x) while the largest cohort in the table (Product Full Review, n=16) sits at 1.67x. That is confounded by naming granularity and cannot carry weight yet, but the store should record instalment index alongside every format so the peak becomes observable rather than argued about.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Contradicted: Corpus (33 channels, 831 videos): near-duplicates median 0.980x vs unique 1.005x (MWU z=-1.68, p=0.093). Age-adjusted the gap widens against repetition: 0.954x vs 1.016x (n=278 vs 534, z=-2.67, p=0.0076). Only 15 of 33 channels had repeats beating uniques. Our channels on first-28d views: repeated 0.99x (n=18) vs unique 1.00x (n=101), p=0.95. Conditional test, strict format frames (signature carrying >=2 literal frame words): 9 pairs where the prior instance scored >=1.5x produced follow-ups with median 1.01x and 0 of 9 reaching 1.5x (base rate 7%); median ratio next/prev = 0.29. Our channels: 3 such pairs, next median 0.72x, ratio 0.45, 0 of 3 reaching 1.5x.

Caveat: Signature repetition is a proxy for 'near-duplicate of a proven format' and catches generic title habits as well as deliberate franchises; a creator could execute the 90/10 rule without the title showing it. The conditional test that isolates deliberate repeats-of-a-hit is the strongest evidence but rests on only 12 pairs. Regression to the mean guarantees some decline from a >=1.5x instance regardless of format logic — but the claim asserts near-duplicates beat wholly new videos, and they do not beat them even before conditioning on a prior hit.

Where the claim came from
With a meme, you already know 90% of the joke. In this case, you know that grumpy Cat is grumpy, Ohanian told me. What makes it funny is the 10% twist, or what the caption is.

packaging

2 claims
Candidate Law packaging · earlier check spanned 42 channels
weak Correlation The trigger and the outcome move together on the channels measured. That is a pattern, not a cause. held 42% of 19 measurements 19 channels
Ideal title length is a myth — character count creates neither relevance, clarity, nor desire, and different surfaces truncate differently; the correct test is the complete package judged at realistic feed size.
Source: idea-engine research dossier
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is length a CAUSE or a PROXY? Our own corpus says it is a proxy whose sign flips by niche — 'title over 60 chars' scores 0.90x vs 1.00x in maker-builds and 0.72x vs 1.00x in roblox, but 1.04x vs 0.97x in motorcycle (n=127, the largest cell in the table). The discriminating question is therefore: does this niche's demand arrive by BROWSE or by SEARCH? In browse-driven niches the long title is a symptom of two crammed concepts (Brag's actual mechanism) and reads as noise at feed size; in spec-driven search niches the extra characters are the brand/model/year the viewer typed, so length correlates with matching rather than with confusion. Reframe both claims as 'one concept per title' (causal) and drop the character count entirely (non-causal).

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Checked: Niche-level rho: maker-builds +0.047 (n=330, p=0.40), motorcycle +0.128 (n=406, p=0.009), roblox +0.036 (n=378, p=0.48). Per-channel the sign is a coin flip: 21 of 42 channels positive, 21 negative; only 6 reach p<0.05 and they split both ways (Motovudu +0.71, MotoJitsu +0.55, TwoWheelObsession +0.54, William Osman +0.40 vs KreekCraft -0.66, Kat -0.49). Bucket medians run in OPPOSITE directions by niche: motorcycle rises monotonically (<30 chars 0.87x -> 70+ chars 1.11x) while roblox falls off a cliff at the top (60-69 chars 0.80x, 70+ 0.26x on n=3).

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. Outlier score is a views measure, not CTR — a length effect that lives purely in click-through with impressions compensating would be invisible here. Also, length is confounded with format: motorcycle's long titles are largely episodic travel series with a loyal returning audience, so 'longer works' there may be 'series work there'. The claim survives because no consistent direction exists, which is weaker evidence than a demonstrated null with tight confidence intervals.

Character count does not create relevance, clarity, or desire. Different surfaces truncate differently.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Supported: rho(28d views, APV) is negative in 6/6 channels: Channel C -0.47, Channel D -0.46, Channel E -0.73, Channel A -0.49, Channel F -0.83, Channel G -0.61. Pooled -0.54 (n=119). Controlling duration barely moves it (pooled -0.51; per-channel -0.42 to -0.84). The top-view video sits below its channel's mean APV in 6/6 channels (e.g. Channel C 24.8% vs mean 46.7%; Channel A 21.9% vs 41.4%). Top-3-by-views median APV vs bottom-3: Channel C 29.7% vs 46.7%, Channel A 26.5% vs 45.7%, Channel E 25.7% vs 37.2%.

Caveat: This is CORRELATION only. We observe that high-view videos hold less; we cannot observe WHY. The stated mechanism (wider reach imports less-sticky viewers) is untested — a rival explanation fits the same data: high-view videos here are also longer (pooled rho views~duration +0.23, duration~APV -0.30), and broad-appeal topics may simply be structurally looser. Controlling duration leaves the effect nearly intact, which weakens but does not eliminate that rival. The repackaging half of the claim is untestable: we hold no before/after repackage events.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Checked: (a) rho(duration, views) positive in 5/6 channels (+0.12 to +0.36), negative only for Channel G (-0.19); pooled +0.23. (b) Longest quartile beats shortest quartile on median 28d views in 5/6: Channel C 426k vs 282k, Channel D 71k vs 44k, Channel E 617k vs 508k, Channel A 304k vs 214k, Channel F 943k vs 618k; Channel G is the exception (485k vs 641k). (c) Corpus rho(duration, outlier score): maker-builds +0.10 (n=330), motorcycle +0.04 (n=406), roblox -0.08 (n=378).

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. Strong selection confound: creators choose length to fit the material, so a big ambitious build gets both more minutes and more interest. The corpus test — which removes channel-size effects — finds essentially NOTHING (rho +0.10 / +0.04 / -0.08), which is the honest reading: length is not a penalty, but it is also not a lever. The claim's own evidence ('longest curves were disproportionately high-view') is exactly the confounded within-channel version.

Evidence and caveats →
Measurement record

Tested as: carrying more than one sponsor read in a video → share of viewers retained to the halfway mark (the claim predicts this goes down)

The question put to the data: Do videos carrying more than one sponsor read hold fewer viewers to the halfway mark?

Exact arithmetic: Median audience share at 50% through for videos with two or more detected sponsor reads, minus the same for videos with one or none.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up. One dot per channel — 2 earlier readings were superseded by a later re-measurement of the same channel and are not drawn.
